cards.body:
*Lesson 0.1 · Think Like an Automator*

_≈ 90 minutes · with Emeka_

Before you build anything, you need to see work the way a machine would: as triggers, steps and outcomes. This module teaches you to find the work worth automating and prove it's worth the effort.

*Your problem:* You know AI and automation matter, but you don't know which tasks to start with.
*The plan:* Map a real process step by step, score each step, and pick the three worth automating first.
*After this lesson:* You can look at any business and say what to automate first, and why.

*Monday at Harvest Lane*

*7:40 a.m.:* 63 unread WhatsApp messages. Orders, questions, a voice note about pepper prices.

*11:20 a.m.:* Still copying. Every order goes into a notebook, then a calculator, then a message back to the customer.

*2:05 p.m.:* A copying mistake. Wrong delivery, a refund, and an unhappy regular customer. Glitch loves manual work.

*6:30 p.m.:* Bolt shows up. "But first," says Bolt, "we find out which parts those are."

*Every automation has three parts*

A *trigger* is the event that starts it. *Actions* are the steps that run after. The *outcome* is the result a person cares about. If you can't name all three, you're not ready to build.

*Think of a bank standing order.* Trigger: the 1st of the month. Action: move ₦20,000 to your landlord. Outcome: rent paid, and you never had to remember.

- *Trigger*: The event that starts a run: a new message, a new row, a time of day.
- *Action*: One thing the automation does: create, update, send, calculate.
- *Workflow*: The whole chain. Zapier calls it a Zap, Make a scenario, n8n a workflow.
- *Run*: One time the workflow fires. 270 orders a week means 270 runs.

*Rules, AI, or agent: use the simplest that works*

Not every task needs AI. Pick the lowest level on this ladder that does the job. Each step up adds power, cost and ways to go wrong.

*Sage:* If a rule can do it, don't wake me up. I'm slower, I cost money per message, and I sometimes guess. Save me for the messy parts.

*Is the task FRIED? Then automate it*

A task is a strong candidate when it matches most of these five signs. Check any task against them before scoring it.

- *F*: Frequent Happens daily or many times a week.
- *R*: Rule-describable You can explain it to a new hire in a few sentences.
- *I*: Input is digital The information already lives in an app, message or file.
- *E*: Errors cost money Mistakes cause refunds, delays or angry customers.
- *D*: Dull Nobody wants to do it and nobody learns from doing it.

*A quick test:* "Copy every order into the notebook" is FRIED on all five. "Decide whether to give a loyal customer credit this month" fails R and D. It needs judgment and a relationship, so a person keeps it.

*Map the process before you touch a tool*

A process map lists every step from trigger to outcome, in order, with who does each one. A *swimlane* map gives each person or system its own row, so handoffs between people become visible. Handoffs are where orders get lost.

- *Write steps as verb + object*: "Check payment", not "payment stuff".
- *One start, one end*: Start at the trigger; end at the outcome.
- *Diamonds for decisions*: Any yes/no question gets its own shape.
- *Map what really happens*: Not what should happen. Ask the person who does it.

*The Automation Score*

FRIED tells you _whether_ a task is a candidate. The score tells you _which one first_. It weighs how much time a task eats, how much damage its mistakes do, and how hard it is to automate.

Weighted minutes =

_runs per week_

×

_minutes per run_

×

_error factor_

Priority score = weighted minutes ÷

_difficulty_

error factor: low ×1 · medium ×1.5 · high ×2

difficulty: easy ÷1 · medium ÷2 · hard ÷3

*Worked row:* "Copy order into notebook" runs 270 times a week, takes 1 minute, and mistakes are costly (×2). Weighted minutes = 270 × 1 × 2 = 540. It's easy to replace (÷1), so priority = 540.

Then check two more things the score can't see:

- *Dependencies*: Some steps can't be automated until an earlier one is. You can't auto-calculate an order the system can't read.
- *A messy process*: Automating chaos gives you faster chaos. Fix the steps first, then automate them.
- *Relationship work*: Negotiating, comforting, deciding on credit. Keep a person here and let automation prepare the facts.

cards.body:
*Solved problem: find Harvest Lane's first three automations*

*The problem.* Tolu handles about 45 orders a day, six days a week (270 a week). The admin eats nearly four hours a day. Which three automations should come first, and are they worth it?

*Step 1 · Collect a week of real data*

Bolt asks Tolu to keep a simple diary for one week: every admin step, how often it happens, and how long it takes. Guessing is fine for the first pass, but a real week beats a guess. Tolu also rates how bad a mistake is at each step, and Bolt rates how hard each step is to automate.

*Step 2 · Score every step*

Apply the formula from Card 5 to each row.

*1:* Read the WhatsApp order · 270 · 0.5 · 135 · Low ×1 · 135 · Hard ÷3 · 45
*2:* Copy order into notebook · 270 · 1 · 270 · High ×2 · 540 · Easy ÷1 · 540
*3:* Work out the total · 270 · 0.5 · 135 · High ×2 · 270 · Easy ÷1 · 270
*4:* Send total and bank details · 270 · 0.5 · 135 · Med ×1.5 · 203 · Easy ÷1 · 203
*5:* Check payment in bank app · 270 · 1 · 270 · High ×2 · 540 · Medium ÷2 · 270
*6:* Plan the rider's route · 6 · 20 · 120 · Med ×1.5 · 180 · Medium ÷2 · 90
*7:* Update the stock sheet · 270 · 0.5 · 135 · Med ×1.5 · 203 · Easy ÷1 · 203
*8:* Send a thank-you message · 270 · 0.25 · 68 · Low ×1 · 68 · Easy ÷1 · 68
*9:* Weekly sales summary · 1 · 90 · 90 · Med ×1.5 · 135 · Easy ÷1 · 135
- *Total admin time* · 1,358 · ≈ 22.6 hours a week
*Step 3 · Rank by priority*

*Step 4 · Check dependencies and redesign the input*

A ranking alone would say "automate step 2 first". But step 2 (copy the order) needs the order in a clean shape, and step 1 (reading a messy WhatsApp message) is hard. Automating step 2 alone isn't possible.

*Sage:* *The key move: change the input, not only the steps.* If customers order through a short order form (or a WhatsApp menu with fixed options), step 1 stops being hard. The order arrives already structured. Now steps 1, 2, 3 and 4 collapse into one automation. Later, in Module 0.5, AI will let Tolu accept free-text orders too.

*Step 5 · Choose three and justify each*

AUTOMATION A · STEPS 1–4

*Order capture*

Order form → new row in the Orders sheet → total calculated by formula → automatic reply with total and bank details. Saves 675 min/week.

AUTOMATION B · STEP 5

*Payment confirmation*

Use a payment link from a provider that sends a signal when money lands. The order row updates to "Paid" by itself. Saves 270 min/week. Built in Track 1–2.

AUTOMATION C · STEP 7

*Stock update*

Rides on A's clean data: each paid order reduces stock per product. Saves 135 min/week, and ends overselling.

*What stays manual, on purpose:* route planning (step 6) happens only six times a week and needs local judgment. The thank-you (step 8) and weekly summary (step 9) are easy quick wins to add once A exists, but they don't hurt enough to go first.

*Step 6 · Estimate the payback*

- *18 h* saved per week (1,080 of 1,358 minutes)
- *4.6 h* of admin left each week, down from 22.6 h
- *₦193,500* monthly value if Tolu's hour is worth ₦2,500 (18 × 2,500 × 4.3 weeks)

Tool costs for these three automations start at zero on free plans and stay small at this volume. Even if building them takes Tolu 20 hours of learning, the time pays back within the first two weeks. _Figures are illustrative; your Silver mission uses your own numbers._

*Why this approach works*

- It starts from measured pain, not from the tool.
- The error factor puts costly mistakes first, not only slow tasks.
- Checking dependencies turns a ranked list into a buildable plan.
- Redesigning the input made the hardest step disappear.

*Common mistakes to avoid*

- Automating the most annoying task instead of the most costly one.
- Mixing units (minutes per month for one row, per week for others).
- Multiplying by difficulty instead of dividing.
- Automating a step that only exists because of a bad earlier step.

*Glitch hunt*

*Glitch:* I scored Tolu's supplier tasks for you. My top pick is obviously the best. Hehehe.

_Task · Runs · Min/run · Error · Difficulty · Glitch's score_
- *Negotiate bulk price with hotel buyer* · 2 / month · 60 · High ×2 · Hard ×3 · 720
- *Email supplier the weekly restock list* · 1 / week · 25 · Med ×1.5 · Easy ×1 · 38
- Record supplier deliveries in stock sheet · 12 / week · 4 · High ×2 · Easy ×1 · 96

Find the three mistakes Glitch made, then re-rank the tasks.

cards.prompt: Made your call on each one? Tap Reveal to check.
cards.answer:
1. *Difficulty multiplied instead of divided.* Glitch wrote ×3. Hard tasks should score lower, not higher.
2. *Mixed units.* Negotiation runs 2 a month, about 0.5 a week. Correct: 0.5 × 60 × 2 ÷ 3 = 20.
3. *Relationship work.* Negotiation fails the R and D in FRIED. Even with the right maths it shouldn't be automated. Automation can prepare the price history for the meeting instead.

*Correct ranking:* record supplier deliveries (96), email restock list (38), negotiation (20, keep manual).

cards.title: Bronze (+25 XP): Map one task you repeat every day
cards.body:
- Choose a task you did at least three times this week.
- Write it as 5–10 steps, each as verb + object.
- Label the trigger, the outcome, and every tool or app you touch.
- Run it through FRIED: how many of the five letters does it hit?

*Done when:*
- Someone else could follow your steps without asking a question.

cards.answer:
*Task:* Sending a monthly invoice to a client. *Trigger:* the 25th of the month. *Outcome:* invoice received and logged.

1. Open last month's invoice file.
2. Duplicate it and rename it.
3. Update date, invoice number and hours.
4. Recalculate the total.
5. Export to PDF.
6. Write the email and attach the PDF.
7. Log the invoice in the tracking sheet.

*FRIED:* F no (monthly), R yes, I yes, E yes, D yes. Four of five: a good candidate, but low frequency, so check its score before building.

cards.title: Silver (+50 XP): Score five processes and pick one
cards.body:
- Use the calculator below with five tasks from your work or business. Replace the three example rows.
- Pick your top task and write three sentences: why it scores high, what it depends on, and one change to its input that would make it easier.

_(Details on screen in the app.)_

*Done when:*
- All five rows use per-week units, and your justification names at least one dependency.

cards.title: Gold (+100 XP): Swimlane a real process and make the case
cards.body:
- Pick a process involving at least two people or teams in a real business (yours, a friend's, or a local shop).
- Interview the person who does it. Map what actually happens as a swimlane, with decisions as diamonds.
- Circle every handoff. Mark where things get lost or delayed.
- Score the steps, choose the first automation, and write a one-paragraph case with weekly hours saved and monthly value.

*Done when:*
- The map has at least two lanes, one decision and one marked handoff.
- The case includes a payback estimate and names one step you'll keep manual, with the reason.

cards.answer:
*Business:* a small pharmacy restocking fast-moving drugs. *Lanes:* counter staff, pharmacist, supplier.

*Finding:* counter staff note low stock on paper; the pharmacist collects the notes on Friday; the supplier gets a phone call. Two handoffs, and the paper notes go missing.

*First automation:* a shared low-stock form that adds to a restock sheet and emails the supplier a list every Thursday. Saves about 2.5 hours a week and cuts stock-outs.

*Kept manual:* choosing substitute brands. It needs the pharmacist's judgment.

cards.q: Which part of an automation starts a run?
cards.why: The trigger is the event (a new message, a new row, a time) that starts every run.

cards.q: Which task is the weakest candidate for automation?
options: Copying form responses into a sheet
Sending a receipt when a payment lands
Deciding whether to give a loyal customer credit after a bad month
cards.why: It fails R and D in FRIED: it needs judgment and a relationship. Automation can gather the facts; a person decides.

cards.q: A task runs 50 times a week, takes 3 minutes, errors are costly (high ×2), and it's easy to automate. What's its priority score?
Why did Tolu group steps 1–4 into one automation?
options: Because steps 2–4 depend on the order being readable first
Because they had the highest scores
Because AI can do all of them
cards.why: Dependencies: you can't copy or total an order the system can't read. Changing the input to a form removed the hard step.

cards.q: A process is messy and done differently every time. What should you do first?
options: Automate it quickly to save time
Add an AI agent to handle the variety
Map it and simplify the steps, then automate
cards.why: Automating a messy process only gives you a faster mess. Fix it, then automate.

cards.body:
*Remember this*

1. Every automation is trigger → actions → outcome.
2. Use the simplest level that works: rules, then AI, then agents.
3. If a task is FRIED (frequent, rule-describable, input digital, errors costly, dull), it's a candidate.
4. Map what really happens, lane by lane. Handoffs are where work gets lost.
5. Priority = runs × minutes × error factor ÷ difficulty, all per week.
6. Check dependencies and fix the input before you automate.

*Lesson 0.1 complete!* _Think Like an Automator_ is done and saved to your progress, on WhatsApp and in the app.

Next up: Lesson 0.2, _How Apps Talk: APIs & Webhooks_.
